name: Tap water / fluoride avoidance

lead: Some appearance-focused people avoid tap water to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine, presenting it as part of a skin and health routine. Health bodies such as the WHO and CDC support fluoridation at recommended levels, while critics dispute its benefit and safety.
Fluoride is added to public water to reduce tooth decay, with a US recommended level of 0.7 mg/L. No study has tested whether avoiding fluoride changes how someone looks.

paras: People use home filters, bottled or spring water for drinking and cooking, and sometimes shower filters for washing. It is a permanent household switch rather than a short course.

Fluoridation's documented adverse effect at recommended levels is mostly mild dental fluorosis. Neurodevelopment concerns are debated, and a 2024 US court ruling addressed IQ risk. Reduced fluoride exposure is associated with more cavities in some reviews.

angle.text: Some appearance-focused users drink and wash with filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, aiming for healthier skin and teeth. Health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no study has looked at appearance.

lead: Tap water / fluoride avoidance is a practice in which people drink and sometimes wash with filtered, bottled or spring water instead of municipal tap water, mainly to avoid fluoride and sometimes chlorine. In appearance-focused communities it is presented as part of a routine aimed at keeping teeth, skin and overall health looking their best.

The clearest appearance link is dental fluorosis, a change in tooth enamel caused by swallowing too much fluoride while teeth are forming. It ranges from faint white flecks to brown mottling and pitting, and the greatest risk is from birth to about age six [1]. Avoiding extra fluoride sources during those years is how some parents and adults frame the practice; after about age seven, most permanent teeth have finished developing and the risk falls substantially [1].

Water fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to public supplies to reduce tooth decay; the US recommended level is 0.7 mg/L [2]. The WHO, FDI World Dental Federation and US CDC endorse it as safe and effective at recommended levels, while opponents argue the benefit is small and safety uncertain [2][3]. No published study has tested fluoride avoidance for facial appearance or skin.
infobox: Dental fluorosis (enamel spotting) during tooth development [1]

paras: Fluoride is added to public water mainly as sodium fluoride, fluorosilicic acid or sodium fluorosilicate; it does not change the water's taste, smell or look [2]. Grand Rapids, Michigan, began fluoridating on January 25, 1945, the first city to do so, after decades of research into the staining of teeth in areas with naturally fluoride-rich water [2].

Some countries and cities, including Finland, Germany, Japan, the Netherlands and Switzerland, do not fluoridate or have stopped; Basel, for example, uses fluoridated salt [2]. Israel dropped mandatory fluoridation in 2014 [2][3].

Wikipedia describes dental fluorosis as ranging from small chalky-white spots covering less than a quarter of a tooth, through whole-surface mottling and brown staining, to pitting in severe cases. Most cases are very mild or mild, and sources include naturally fluoride-rich water, certain crops and soil, and supplements; toothpaste is not strongly linked [1].

Cosmetic options described include whitening for mild cases, microabrasion for moderate ones, and composite fillings, veneers or crowns for severe cases [1]. The 2024 Cochrane update of the water fluoridation review set out to evaluate the association of water fluoridation with dental fluorosis alongside its effect on cavities [4]. Cochrane's earlier estimate was that about 12 percent of people at 0.7 ppm had fluorosis of aesthetic concern, mostly mild [2].

sections.h: Positions of health bodies and critics
paras: The WHO, FDI and US CDC endorse fluoridation, and the CDC named it one of the ten great public health achievements of the 20th century in 1999 [2][3]. A 2015 Cochrane review estimated 35% fewer cavities in baby teeth and 26% in permanent teeth in children, but rated the evidence as low quality and found no conclusive adult research [2][3].

The 2011 European Commission review saw no clear advantage over topical fluoride, and the 2007 Nuffield Council on Bioethics found good evidence for or against lacking [2][3]. Opponents raise consent, cost-effectiveness, precaution and conflict-of-interest arguments [3]. In September 2024 a US federal judge ruled in Food and Water Watch v. EPA that fluoridation posed an unreasonable risk of reduced IQ in children, requiring an EPA regulatory response [3].

Some people who avoid tap water are also reacting to chlorine or mineral content. Wikipedia reports that hard drinking water may increase childhood eczema prevalence, though water softeners did not reduce symptoms once the condition was established, and that hard water reduces soap lathering [5]. These points concern minerals, not fluoride.

Dental fluorosis is the only clear adverse effect at recommended levels. Little effect on fracture risk and no clear link to cancer has been reported, and rare acute poisonings have followed improper dosing, including a fatal 1992 Alaska outbreak [2].

Looksmax.org has threads asking whether tap water is harmful and listing what users say is in it [6][7]. Practitioners cite avoiding fluoride and chlorine as a reason for filtered or spring water; see Filtered / spring water. Published sources do not link fluoride avoidance to facial appearance.
No studies found on fluoride avoidance and facial appearance. Studies of water fluoridation concern dental and general health outcomes, summarised above [2][3][4].
